title: Breathing & Mindfulness for Little Ones
strapline: Tiny, playful moments of noticing and slow breathing — pausing to smell the flower, blow the candle, and feel calm arrive.
intent: Children discover that slowing their breath changes how their body feels — a calming tool they carry everywhere for free.
Children practise paying attention to the here and now — a sound, a texture, their own breath — building focus and calm.
Children learn playful breathing techniques while relaxed, so the tool is ready when big feelings come.
Children develop early self-awareness, noticing their heartbeat, their tummy rising, their busy or still mind.
Children experience unhurried, peaceful moments in a fast day — a right to stillness.
implementation: Make breathing concrete and playful: 'smell the flower, blow out the candle', 'blow the dandelion', trace a finger up and down a star as you breathe.
Keep sessions tiny and frequent — a minute of belly breaths before group time — rather than expecting long stillness from little bodies.
Anchor attention with props: a feather to keep afloat, a pinwheel to spin slowly, a soft toy riding a tummy up and down.
Model it genuinely yourself, out loud — 'I'm feeling rushed, I'm going to take three slow breaths' — so it's real, not a lesson.
Invite noticing through the senses: 'what can you hear right now? what does the rug feel like?' — mindfulness as curiosity.
Never force stillness — offer it, make it inviting, and let children opt in; a wriggly child at the edge is still absorbing it.
key_questions: Can you smell the flower slowly, then blow out the candle?
What can you hear if we go very quiet?
Can you feel your tummy going up and down?
How does your body feel after our slow breaths?
Where in your body do you feel calm?

impact.text: Children regulate big feelings using strategies — including slow breathing — that work for them.
Children know their own feelings have names and have at least one thing that helps them calm.
Children shift and sustain their attention, tuning into the present moment.
Children begin to know what their body needs and do something about it.
Children explore forces and change — breath moving a feather, a pinwheel turning — through calm play.

enhancements: A basket of breathing props — pinwheels, feathers, bubbles — children choose from for their own calm moment.
A 'breathing shapes' poster: trace a finger round a square or up a mountain, breathing with the line.
A short lying-down 'listening to the rain' or 'floppy like a rag doll' relaxation after busy play.
Bubble-blowing outdoors as a whole-group slow-breathing game.
A calm-jar and a comfy cushion so breathing and the calm-down corner work together.

playing_exploring: Children explore breath through play — floating feathers, spinning pinwheels, blowing bubbles.
Noticing sounds, textures and their own body invites open sensory curiosity.
active_learning: Feeling calmer after breathing rewards children for pausing, building the habit.
Children choose to use their breathing when they need it, showing ownership.
creating_thinking: Children make the link between slow breathing and a calmer body.
They begin to notice and describe their inner state — the root of self-awareness.
